newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian inflation up, riel keeps slipping.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian inflation up, riel keeps slipping.

text.p: Cambodian inflation surged and the riel continued its slide in value in October as the country contended with the aftermath of floods and growing political tensions, government economists said on Wednesday.

The worst flooding in two years caused the consumer price index to rise 6.2 percent in October for all food and beverages, and vegetable prices in some areas nearly doubled, said Khay Phousnith of the central bank's economic research department.
Newly released central bank figures for the month showed the inflation rate across all categories was 7.1 percent, up from 6.8 percent in September.

The floods of late September and October, which left half a million people short of food and affected 200,000 hectares (500,000 acres) of rice fields, could cut gross domestic product (GDP) growth by one percent this year, Sok Hach, economic adviser for the Finance Ministry, recently told Reuters.
Damage from the floods could cost $30 million.
Cambodia's GDP growth, forecast at seven percent for the year, would now be closer to six percent, he said.
The country's per capita GDP of $300 is among Asia's lowest.

In October, the riel depreciated to 2,742 to the dollar, continuing its gradual but steady decrease in value over the past year and a half. Last June, the riel was valued at 2,375, but has lost value each month since.
In August, the riel plummeted to 3,000 against the dollar, prompting the government to intervene to stabilise the currency.
Concern about the riel flared again this month when a letter from the National Bank was leaked to the press indicating foreign reserves had fallen and the riel could be destabilised.
National Bank officials have since said the reserves have returned to reasonable levels (about $146 million), though they remain close to the minimum levels set by the International Monetary Fund.

Perceived political instability also threatens the riel, analysts said. On Tuesday, the brother-in-law of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen was shot dead, and tensions within the ruling coalition are high. The killing is believed to have been politically motivated.
One analyst said the riel could continue to slide through to the next general elections, scheduled for 1998.
